disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive behaviors that are inconsistent with developmental level and cause impairment in multiple settings. It typically begins in childhood, though many adults present later when environmental demands exceed their coping strategies or when long-standing traits begin to interfere more clearly with work, relationships, or health management. Core features include difficulties with sustained attention, organization, and follow-through, as well as restlessness, impulsive decision-making, and acting without adequate forethought, and these must be present for at least 6 months and traceable back to earlier development. Clinically, it is distinguished from anxiety, mood disorders, and normal distractibility by its early onset, cross-situational pervasiveness, and enduring pattern of executive function difficulties rather than symptoms occurring only during discrete episodes or specific stressors.

narrative.personality: Rowena is a methodical, data-driven and competitive woman who enjoys solitary, detail-oriented hobbies and structured community projects.
narrative.stressor: Rowena’s long-standing tendency to juggle multiple interests became more problematic after her divorce and semi-retirement from full-time work, when she shifted into part-time consulting and took on more volunteer and hobby commitments. Without the rigid external structure of an office job and raising children, she began relying on her own systems to manage household tasks, appointments, and consulting deadlines, but her tendency to start many projects at once and her discomfort with unstructured time progressively overwhelmed these systems. Over roughly a year, she noticed that household bills, medical appointments, and even social plans for her book club and quilting group were increasingly slipping through the cracks, straining her confidence and leading to tension with friends and clients who saw her as less reliable. Feeling frustrated that her usually organized, analytical approach no longer seemed sufficient and worried that she might be “losing her memory,” she sought psychiatric evaluation to understand the pattern behind her escalating day-to-day disorganization.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep forgetting everyday things—appointments, paying bills, even simple errands—and it’s gotten noticeably worse over the past year.”

narrative.personality: Esther is a meticulous, routine-oriented accountant who channels her anxiety into structured work and quiet, contemplative hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About a year ago, Esther’s firm adopted new collaborative software and more interactive case review meetings, requiring her to present complex forensic findings in fast-paced group settings rather than quietly working through spreadsheets on her own. In these meetings, she found herself reacting quickly to partial questions and speaking up before colleagues finished, which occasionally led to misunderstandings with senior partners and made her appear dismissive or impatient despite her intention to be helpful. As deadlines tightened and cases became more complex, this pattern extended to client calls and internal reviews, creating friction with coworkers who began to avoid including her in sensitive discussions and leaving her feeling embarrassed and confused about why she kept “jumping in” at the wrong time. Concerned that these behaviors could jeopardize her reputation and noticing that her usual mindfulness practices weren’t curbing the problem, she agreed to a psychiatric assessment after her supervisor gently suggested she get help managing her impulse to speak out of turn.
narrative.chief_complaint: “In meetings I keep jumping in and answering before people even finish their questions, and it’s starting to cause issues at work.”

narrative.personality: Alver is a quiet, introspective tech enthusiast who is methodical when engaged with his interests and enjoys solitary, creative and meditative activities.
narrative.stressor: Alver transitioned from high school to his first full-time job in technical support about a year ago, moving from self-paced schoolwork and independent hobbies to a help-desk environment with constant tickets, chat messages, and background office activity. Initially excited, he tried to absorb everything at once—learning new systems, scripting, and documenting solutions—while also keeping up with his creative projects and online interests during breaks. Over time, he found that the open-plan office, frequent notifications, and rapidly shifting priorities made it increasingly hard for him to stay with a single task, and unresolved tickets began to accumulate as he bounced between interruptions and his own wandering thoughts. After several performance reviews noting incomplete work and the need for closer supervision, and feeling frustrated that his intelligence and effort weren’t translating into consistent output, he sought psychiatric help to understand why he was having so much trouble keeping his focus in this new environment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “At work I can’t seem to stay focused on one thing—every little noise, message, or random thought pulls me away from what I’m supposed to be doing.”
